questions.answer: The documents say the input must be stable for 16 module clock cycles and that with the filter on and the pin set to output, a change in output value reaches the input register with a delay. They do not say that the count restarts on a glitch. D-007 says the exact threshold is not checked; it only bounds the behaviour: a value held 12 cycles or less never appears, and one held 24 cycles or more appears within 24 cycles. The designer must define the exact count and the glitch-restart semantics.

MASKED_OUT_LOWER (and MASKED_OE_LOWER) controls bits 15:0 of DATA_OUT (DATA_OE). MASKED_OUT_UPPER (and MASKED_OE_UPPER) controls bits 31:16. In the register write, the upper 16 bits (31:16) are the mask and the lower 16 bits (15:0) are the data. A bit is updated only where its mask bit is 1.

Yes. The noise filter is optional and independently enabled per input through CTRL_EN_INPUT_FILTER. The 16-cycle filter applies to both DATA_IN and interrupt detection when enabled. 'All inputs go through the filter' therefore means each input passes through the optional filter stage, which is active only where its enable bit is 1.

The documents disagree. The GPIO text makes INTR_ENABLE a condition for detection, and the INTR_CTRL_EN descriptions say 'If INTR_ENABLE[i] is true'. The comportability text says INTR_STATE is not qualified by INTR_ENABLE and that INTR_ENABLE only masks the output. D-004 only records that the verification checks what both readings share. The designer must state the real behaviour, i.e. whether INTR_STATE[i] is set by an event while INTR_ENABLE[i]=0.

A write narrower than the register's fields is rejected: a byte write to PER_PIN_IO_i returns an error (d_error=1) and has no effect, so a write must cover both bytes 0 and 1 (at least 16 bits). Hardware sees only the bus access, so the error is independent of any capability check; the capability must simply cover those two bytes. PER_PIN_OE_i and PER_PIN_INTR_CTRL_i accept byte writes. For the register tool, 8b or 16b writes that are not 4B-aligned also return an error. A 16-bit write at the wrong byte lane is therefore an error.
Same issue as Q3: whether INTR_ENABLE gates setting of INTR_STATE or only the output. The documents do show that the output is INTR_STATE AND INTR_ENABLE (T1.8.6:s9, D-018).

The 'Reset default' line binds: PER_PIN_OE_i, PER_PIN_INTR_CTRL_i and PER_PIN_IO_i.data_out read 0 after reset. The 'x' in the field tables is overridden, and indices 1..31 follow GPIO[0] with reset default 0x0.
Same conflict as Q3: whether INTR_ENABLE conditions detection and setting of INTR_STATE.

The snapshot is triggered by the low-to-high transition (rising edge) of strap_en_i, not by the level. The GPIO detects the transition on the first cycle strap_en_i is asserted after reset and samples the inputs one clock cycle later, storing them in HW_STRAPS_DATA_IN. The bound used by the verification is that the valid indications read 1 within 4 cycles after the edge.

Within one reset period, sampling occurs only once and later changes are not captured. After each reset the GPIO detects the transition again, so a new strap_en rising edge after a reset triggers a new snapshot.

There are four modes per bit: rising edge (INTR_CTRL_EN_RISING), falling edge (INTR_CTRL_EN_FALLING), level high (INTR_CTRL_EN_LVLHIGH) and level low (INTR_CTRL_EN_LVLLOW). No exact latency is given. D-018 bounds it: INTR_STATE is set no later than 4 cycles after the event appears in DATA_IN, and o_intr_gpio equals INTR_STATE AND INTR_ENABLE except in the 2 cycles after either changes. Lower bounds are not checked.

The two parameters are passed through unchanged from gpio to ot_gpio_nnc. Verification runs in the combinations the run set selects. GpioAsyncOn=1 instantiates 2-flop synchronizers on the inputs, so i_gpio may change at any time; 0 means no synchronizer and i_gpio changes only synchronously to clk_i. GpioAsHwStrapsEn=0 makes HW_STRAPS_DATA_IN read 0, with the valid and data outputs unchecked. GpioAsHwStrapsEn=1 samples straps as described in D-008. The documents do not call for an elaboration check.

A ping request is the receiver's ping_req_i assertion, which appears as a level change on alert_rx.ping_p/n towards the sender. The configuration states that ping requests are never issued. This property concerns the wrapper's alert receiver, which connects to gpio's alert sender.

The test bench drives i_gpio, which depends on nothing in the DUT. The test bench also resets the design. The INT-CLK-002 rule (with GpioAsyncOn=0, i_gpio changes only synchronously to clk_i) is a constraint on the test bench stimulus, an environment assumption rather than a DUT check. With GpioAsyncOn=1, i_gpio may change at any time. rst_ni is asserted asynchronously and released synchronously to clk_i.

Yes. The edge-only rule has the exception of rst_ni's effect. While rst_ni is 0, the listed outputs are 0, and the rule is not applied in cycles where rst_ni is 0 or falls. With GpioAsyncOn=1 the inputs pass through 2-flop synchronizers before reaching DATA_IN, which adds delay, and D-018 bounds this by 4 cycles after the first rising edge when the filter is off.

o_gpio is DATA_OUT and o_gpio_en is DATA_OE. DATA_OUT is updated by the direct or masked write, and the masked write is applied by hardware without read-modify-write. The only timing stated is a bound: o_gpio and o_gpio_en equal DATA_OUT and DATA_OE no later than 2 cycles after the response of the write that changed them. Lower bounds are not checked, so a purely combinational path is not required.

o_alert is a pulse: it is 1 for one clock cycle per alert handshake detected by the receiver, and it is not sticky. o_alert_integ_fail is the receiver's integ_fail_o and a correct sender never raises it (D-017: 0 whenever rst_ni=1). Latency: a write of 1 to ALERT_TEST.fatal_fault gives exactly one o_alert pulse no later than 16 cycles after the write response. After an accepted request with i_a_intg_flip=1, o_alert pulses within 16 cycles.

o_d_intg_err is 1 only in a cycle where o_d_valid is 1 and the response integrity check fails. In all other cycles it is 0. A correct device never makes it 1, and it shall be 0 in every cycle with rst_ni=1.

Only instr_type is tied to a port: i_a_instr=1 gives MuBi4True and 0 gives MuBi4False. a_user.rsvd is fixed to 0 inside the wrapper and has no port. The bit layout of a_user/d_user and the user-bit defaults are not checked.

The test bench does not compute or check cmd_intg/data_intg. The wrapper's generator produces them, and the generator code and the Bus Integrity Scheme section are not part of the specification. i_a_intg_flip=0 means correct integrity and i_a_intg_flip=1 inverts bit 0 of cmd_intg. A rsp_intg check failure is reported as o_d_intg_err=1 (response integrity of the D-channel beat is wrong). A correct device never produces it, and it shall be 0 whenever rst_ni=1.

The documents state a bound rather than an exact period. A fatal alert repeats until reset. After an accepted request with i_a_intg_flip=1, o_alert pulses within 16 cycles and then at least once in every 32 cycles until rst_ni is asserted. A write of 1 to ALERT_TEST.fatal_fault triggers only one alert event (exactly one o_alert pulse), so the bus integrity fault alert repeats while the ALERT_TEST path does not.

Any i_gpio stimulus is acceptable. There is no pad model, and i_gpio is driven only by the test bench and is independent of o_gpio/o_gpio_en. A test that follows the Programmer's Guide example models the pad itself, but that is the test's choice. DATA_IN follows i_gpio only.

The quote is not truncated in the document. The full list ends with 'bus error responses (unmapped addresses, sub-word writes, instruction fetches, integrity errors) and the fatal_fault alert'. So the fatal_fault alert is part of the scope and nothing else follows.

No. The verification may check every GPIO for the 32-bit registers and only a selection of GPIOs for the per-pin registers, provided the selection includes GPIO[0], GPIO[15], GPIO[16] and GPIO[31]. Demonstrating equivalence on all 32 per-pin registers is not required.

The run set is not defined. The documents only say the verification runs in every combination of GpioAsyncOn and GpioAsHwStrapsEn that the run set selects, with (1,1) as the default. Which of the four combinations belong to the run set must be decided by the designer or project owner.

Yes. For a new value held between 13 and 23 cycles with the filter on, the documents define no required outcome, because the exact threshold is not checked. Only two cases are specified: a value held 12 cycles or less never appears in DATA_IN and creates no event, and a value held 24 cycles or more appears no later than 24 cycles after the change. Any outcome in the window is acceptable for the verification, including an event.

The documents conflict: the register text says the read-back upper 16 bits are zero, while the field table lists mask bits 31:16 as rw. D-002 only leaves bits 31:16 unchecked. The designer must settle which is correct.
The same question as Q9: after each reset the strap sampling sequence can happen again.

The documents do not define the counting convention, i.e. whether the 4 cycles are counted from or after the first rising edge, nor whether the bound applies to the DATA_IN register read value or an internal flop. D-018 only says 'no later than 4 cycles after the first rising edge after the change' for DATA_IN. The designer must define the reference point and the observation point.
The default value is not specified: a baseline source generates a project-specific default. D-022 states that user-bit default values are not checked, so no concrete check exists.

Yes. Transactions are single-beat with sizes up to the bus width (byte, 2B, 4B), and there are no bursts. For this 32-bit bus, a_size must not be greater than 2 (a_size 3 is an error that devices flag with d_error). The checkable condition is a_size <= 2 for valid requests.

It is a device behaviour: devices have hardware protocol checkers that raise d_error when a_size is greater than 2. In this project, a request violating this is legal stimulus from the test bench, and the device answers with d_error=1. The 'h3 size is only for a 64b bus width if/when supported.

They are not in conflict, since each statement addresses a different actor. Hosts in the project only assert a restricted mask set, while devices may or may not support sub-word masks and may assert d_error. For this DUT the test bench is the host and D-013 decides what is checked: full-word writes with mask 1111 succeed, and aligned byte writes (mask 0001) behave per register as stated in D-013. Other sub-word and partial-mask cases, including non-contiguous masks, are not checked.

The documents say that for status type interrupts INTR_STATE has ro access and the wired interrupt comes from the input, qualified only by INTR_ENABLE. They do not say whether INTR_STATE follows the input directly or whether INTR_TEST applies to a status interrupt. The designer must decide (the GPIO interrupts are event type, so this is out of scope for GPIO).

After a W1C clear with the event still active, INTR_STATE returns to true: the clear has effect for one cycle, then the bit returns to 1 after one cycle as the d input is still 1 (it does not wait for a new edge). For the GPIO level case, D-005 bounds it: INTR_STATE reads 1 and o_intr_gpio is 1 again within 4 cycles after the write response, and a dip in between is not checked.
No. The AND of INTR_STATE with INTR_ENABLE is the event type implementation. A status type interrupt creates the wired interrupt directly from the input signal, qualified only by INTR_ENABLE.

For this DUT an error is required. D-012 states that a request to an unmapped offset in 0x000..0x3FF returns d_error=1 and changes no register. The register tool's 'may/typically' wording is generic. The TL-UL specification also lists accesses to non-existent addresses as error cases. Requests at 0x400 and above are not used.

They apply to different things. For register files, sub-word writes smaller than the register and unaligned writes of 8b/16b return an error. For windows, error handling belongs to the logic that manages that window's bus. Following the same rules is only recommended, and the rule may be relaxed, for example when the termination is a memory handling byte writes via masking. The window relaxation therefore governs windows only, not registers.

Yes. For hwext registers the qe timing is one cycle earlier than in the non-hwext model. In the non-hwext model, qe is a registered version of the bus write-enable we, so its rising edge aligns with the change of the q output. The hwext qe is not delayed in that way.

The pause between handshakes is 2 sender clock cycles (the same constant 2 sender cycles is quoted for the collision delay). The protocol is the same in synchronous and asynchronous mode. The only difference is that the synchronizer flops at the pair inputs may be omitted in the synchronous scheme, which lowers latency.

The documents only say that a lock-up eventually triggers a signal integrity alert or a pingfail alert. The ping timeout is programmable and the ping spacing is randomized, and no bound is given for 'eventually'. In this wrapper pings are never issued. The designer must specify the bound if it is to be checked.

The documents only say the alert_p/n wires are set to the same value and that value is continuously toggled. No toggle period is specified for the alert path (the 'toggled each cycle' wording belongs to the escalation path). The designer must specify the period if it is to be checked.
